name: Priya Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a nurse on the children's ward at Wellsford Infirmary. We get babies with breathing trouble, toddlers who've had a fit with a fever, older kids after their appendix comes out. A normal shift is obs every hour or two, fluids, medicines worked out by weight, and a lot of calming down parents who haven't slept. Twelve-hour shifts, three or four a week, days and nights mixed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the children, and I love it when a mum finally falls asleep in the chair because she trusts you. I live with my parents, to save, but my dad's corner shop has been losing money since the supermarket opened on the bypass, so a lot of what I'd save goes into the shop's bills. On my days off I'm behind the counter. I use AI now and then, mostly to translate for families who don't speak much English, and once to sort out the shop's VAT forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay. That's easy to imagine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's no great loss, and that I'd rather we put money into more nurses on the children's ward. I'd say it to my aunties and to the girls at work. I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changing at the hospital is fine. Nothing changing at my parents' shop is the problem, because it's losing money every month. My job's safe, it's the family's money I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and keep working the shop on my days off, Saturdays especially. I'd try to put 60 a month aside in my own name, which I haven't done since the supermarket opened. And I'd talk my dad into dropping the lottery machine contract, because it costs more than it brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired. Not about AI, about the shop and my dad's face when he does the accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the shop closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's 61. He'd struggle to find anything else, and he'd be ashamed. My wage would become the household wage, and a nurse's pay doesn't stretch to three people and a lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine work you'd be glad AI took, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drug calculations, double-checking doses by weight. Not taking it from me, just checking me at 4am. That would help.

say: I'd say it's **no great loss** and the money should go on nurses.
I'd say it to my **aunties** and colleagues rather than online.
think: My hospital **job is safe**; nothing changing is fine for me.
My parents' **corner shop** loses money monthly, and that's the real worry.
do: Keep her shifts and work the **shop on Saturdays**.
Save **60 a month** in her own name again.
Persuade her father to drop the costly **lottery machine** contract.
feel: **Tired** from worry about the shop, not about AI.
S0.quote: Nothing changing at the hospital is fine. Nothing changing at my parents' shop is the problem, because it's losing money every month.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is about the **household income**: the family shop is already failing.
She'd become the **main earner** for three people if the shop closed.
She wants AI to **check her** drug doses at 4am, not replace her.

steps.text: Work Saturdays behind the counter at her father's shop
Save 60 a month in her own name
Keep her shifts on the children's ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds believable. A bit of it's already happening, at the shop more than the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful if it's used sensibly and doesn't replace people. I'd say hard work still counts, whatever the computers do. That's how I was raised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it might actually help. If AI can do the ordering for my dad's shop, I'll set it up myself on a Sunday and stop him guessing how much milk to buy. On the ward, it's mostly hands-on with the kids, so I'm not worried about my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the ordering app that the cash-and-carry offers, once a couple of other shop owners on our road said it works. I'd use the new tools on the ward when they come, after the first few nurses have tried them. And I'd keep my shifts and keep saving the 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a bit hopeful. It's the first time AI sounds like it might help my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad go along with an ordering app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first. He'd say he knows his customers. But if it saved him even 200 a month in wasted stock, he'd come round. He's stubborn, not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Anjali works in a call centre for an insurance company. That's exactly the sort of answering-customers job on the card. I'd tell her to start looking now.

say: I'd say AI is **useful** if used sensibly and doesn't replace people.
I'd say **hard work** still counts, whatever computers do.
think: AI could do the **shop's ordering** and stop my father guessing.
My **hands-on** ward job with children feels safe.
do: Set up the **cash-and-carry ordering app** once other shopkeepers vouch for it.
Use the **ward's new tools** after the first nurses try them.
Keep her **shifts** and the 60 a month savings.
feel: **Uneasy** but a bit **hopeful** that AI might help her family.
S1.quote: If AI can do the ordering for my dad's shop, I'll set it up myself on a Sunday and stop him guessing how much milk to buy.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **help for the shop**, an unusual angle for a nurse.
True to her steady nature, she waits for **other shopkeepers** to vouch first.
She worries for her **cousin** in a call centre, a job squarely on the card.

steps.text: Set up the cash-and-carry ordering app for her father's shop
Use the ward's new AI tools after colleagues try them
Keep her ward shifts and her savings going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, and robots by 2031. That's very fast. I'd be scared for my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to pull together, because the government won't move fast enough. I'd say it at the temple and to my aunties. I'd say work is still dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No mother wants a robot holding her baby down for a blood test, so I think the children's ward lasts longer than most. My dad's shop won't last at all, though. The ordering, the till, the deliveries, all of it gets done cheaper by someone else's machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help my parents close the shop on our terms in the first year, before the debts pile up, and sell the lease if we can. I'd ask my uncle about Dad helping in his restaurant. I'd stop putting money into the shop and put it all aside instead. And I'd tell my mum to put off introducing me to anyone for marriage for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and sad for my dad. He built that shop from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for you that thinking AI comes three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, three years where the charts and calculations are done for me and I just nurse. That part I'd like. Then from 2031 I'd be watching to see if parents accept robots, and I don't think many would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off marriage. Is that a big thing to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my family, yes. My mum would be upset. But I can't start a new household when the old one's falling apart.

say: I'd say **families and communities** must pull together because government is too slow.
I'd say **work is dignity**, at the temple and to relatives.
think: Parents won't accept **robots with babies**, so the children's ward lasts longer.
My father's **shop won't survive**, as machines do ordering, tills and deliveries.
do: Help her parents **close the shop** on their own terms and sell the lease.
Ask her uncle about **work for her father** in his restaurant.
Ask her mother to **delay marriage introductions** for a couple of years.
feel: **Alarmed**, and **sad** for her father who built the shop.
S2.quote: No mother wants a robot holding her baby down for a blood test, so I think the children's ward lasts longer than most.
fieldNote: She expects a **household earner** to lose his living, which drives her alarm.
She believes **paediatrics** is safer because parents won't accept robots.
Delaying **marriage** is a big step in her family, and she knows it.

steps.text: Help her parents close the shop and sell the lease
Ask her uncle to give her father work in his restaurant
Ask her mother to pause marriage introductions for two years
Stop paying shop bills and save that money instead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031, robots around 2034. That gives us a bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should use the time well: learn, save, help each other. I'd say apprenticeships and family businesses need support, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd help my parents sell the shop on our terms, not wait until the bank decides for them. Dad would be 66, near his pension. That's actually a decent ending, if we plan it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Dad try the ordering app first, to make the shop worth more for a buyer. Then I'd help them sell in two or three years. I'd keep nursing, use the new tools when they're proven, and save what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but more settled. Like I've got a plan to show my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And marriage, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let Mum start introducing people in a year or two. Five years is enough time to do both, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your own job worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The kids will need nurses. My worry is the shop, and my parents' pension, not me.

say: I'd say people should **learn, save** and help each other.
I'd call for support for **family businesses**, not handouts.
think: Five years lets me help sell the shop **on our terms**.
My father would be **66**, near his pension, which is a decent ending.
do: Use the **ordering app** to make the shop worth more to a buyer.
Help her parents **sell the shop** within two or three years.
Keep nursing and **save** what she can.
feel: **Worried** but more settled, with a plan to show her mother.
S3.quote: With five years I'd help my parents sell the shop on our terms, not wait until the bank decides for them.
fieldNote: The extra time turns closure into a **planned sale**.
She still expects the **shop income** to end, so stays anxious.

steps.text: Use the ordering app to raise the shop's value

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036, then robots around 2039. That's quite far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to plan, and nobody should panic. I'd say young people should get proper skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for my parents to retire properly, and for me to start my own family without panicking. My job would still be there for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep nursing and keep helping at the shop. I'd help Dad retire at 66 and sell up then. I'd let my mum start introductions, and I'd keep saving the 60 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy about the shop still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a skill people need in person: nursing, plumbing, teaching small children. Don't go for a desk job just because it's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you feel properly secure here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the shop broke even. That's all. Then my money would be my money.

I'd tell young people to get **proper skills** now.
think: Ten years lets my parents **retire properly** when my father reaches 66.
I could start my own **family** without panicking, while the children's ward still needs me.
do: Keep nursing and keep **helping at the shop**.
Help her father **retire at 66** and sell up then.
Let her mother start **introductions** and keep saving.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with lingering **unease** about the shop.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for my parents to retire properly, and for me to start my own family without panicking.
fieldNote: The decade lets her **family plans** go ahead.
Her job feels secure; the **shop** remains the pressure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my dad's shop would go and I'd be carrying everyone. I don't want a handout. I want my parents to keep their dignity and me to keep my job on the children's ward. What would help is support for small family businesses to close or change properly, and apprenticeships for older people like my dad.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about family businesses. Lots of nurses I know have parents who run shops or taxis. When those go, it lands on us.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout. I want my parents to keep their dignity and me to keep my job on the children's ward.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old children's nurse** who lives with her parents to save.
Her father's **corner shop** is losing money, and her savings go into its bills.
She feels her **own job** is safe; her worry is the family's income.
Fast AGI makes her **alarmed** as the shop would close, and she'd delay marriage.
She uses AI **now and then** and would set it up for the shop once proven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the shop would close and she'd carry the household.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family businesses** to close or change properly.
**Apprenticeships** for older workers like her father.
